# Selected worked solutions {#sec-solutions}

These solutions develop a selection of the numbered exercises in Chapters
1–14. Each heading gives the original exercise number and title so that a
reader can return to the question without guessing which calculation is
being discussed. They are best read after attempting the exercise. Open
research questions remain open: the calculations here establish the finite
models and bounds stated in their questions, rather than a general
universality principle.

Throughout this appendix, logarithms are natural except for the explicitly
bit-valued resource measures in Chapter 10. We use
$D(\rho,\sigma)=\frac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1$ and
$S_2(\rho)=-\log\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$.

## Chapter 1: states and information

Return to @sec-states for the definitions of reduced states and distinguishability.

### Exercise 2: Partial trace in components

Write the coefficients as a matrix whose row is the $A$ index and whose
column is the $B$ index:

$$
C=\frac1{\sqrt3}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The partial trace is not an elementwise sum of amplitudes. Its components
are $(\rho_A)_{aa'}=\sum_b C_{ab}C_{a'b}^*$, because tracing identifies the
two bath indices. Thus $\rho_A=CC^\dagger$, while
$\rho_B=C^TC^*$ in this coefficient convention. Here the matrix is real
and symmetric, so both reductions happen to be

$$
\rho_A=\rho_B=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-sol-reduced-example}

Its trace is one and its determinant is $1/9$. The characteristic
polynomial is therefore $x^2-x+1/9$, giving
$\lambda_\pm=(3\pm\sqrt5)/6$. Both are positive and sum to one, as a
density matrix requires. The two reductions have the same nonzero
spectrum because they come from a global pure state; their equality as
matrices in this example is an additional symmetry, not a general rule.

Instead of squaring the eigenvalues separately, use
$\lambda_+^2+\lambda_-^2=(\lambda_++\lambda_-)^2-2\lambda_+\lambda_-=7/9$.
Consequently $S_2(\rho_A)=S_2(\rho_B)=\log(9/7)$. The result is below
$\log2$: the pair is entangled, but its Schmidt weights are unequal.

### Exercise 4: Trace distance

For Bloch vectors $\boldsymbol r,\boldsymbol s$, subtracting the two
density operators gives
$\rho-\sigma=(\boldsymbol r-\boldsymbol s)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma/2$.
The Pauli identity
$(\boldsymbol v\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)^2=|\boldsymbol v|^2I$ follows
because the antisymmetric term
$i\sum_{ijk}v_iv_j\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ vanishes. Hence the difference
has eigenvalues $\pm|\boldsymbol r-\boldsymbol s|/2$. The trace norm adds
their absolute values, so

$$
D(\rho,\sigma)=\frac12|\boldsymbol r-\boldsymbol s|.
$$ {#eq-sol-bloch-distance}

The states $|0\rangle$ and $|+\rangle$ have Bloch vectors $(0,0,1)$ and
$(1,0,0)$, whose separation is $\sqrt2$. Their trace distance is
$1/\sqrt2$. For equally likely preparations, the optimal single-copy
identification probability is $(1+1/\sqrt2)/2$. Measuring along the
direction $(\boldsymbol e_z-\boldsymbol e_x)/\sqrt2$ attains this value:
the optimal observable follows the difference of the two states, rather
than either preparation axis alone.

## Chapter 2: measurement and ensembles

The ensemble moments used below are defined in @sec-measurement-ensembles.

### Exercise 1: Two copies

In the symmetric basis
$\{|00\rangle,|s\rangle=(|01\rangle+|10\rangle)/\sqrt2,|11\rangle\}$,
the pole ensemble gives
$M_2^{(Z)}=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,0,1/2)$. Meanwhile
$|++\rangle$ and $|--\rangle$ have coordinate vectors
$(1/2,\pm1/\sqrt2,1/2)$. Form their projectors before averaging; the terms
linear in the middle coordinate cancel. The result is

$$
M_2^{(X)}=
\begin{pmatrix}1/4&0&1/4\\0&1/2&0\\1/4&0&1/4\end{pmatrix},\qquad
M_2^{(Z)}-M_2^{(X)}=
\begin{pmatrix}1/4&0&-1/4\\0&-1/2&0\\-1/4&0&1/4\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-sol-two-copy-matrices}

The outer $2\times2$ block has eigenvalues $0,1/2$; the middle vector has
eigenvalue $-1/2$. Both moments vanish on the antisymmetric subspace, so
there is no missing fourth eigenvalue contribution. The trace norm of the
difference is one and its trace distance is $1/2$. Receiving two copies
with a shared preparation label therefore allows success probability
$3/4$, even though one copy is exactly $I/2$ under either source. The
shared label is essential: two independently resampled states would both
give $(I/2)^{\otimes2}$.

### Exercise 2: POVM versus instrument

An effect fixes a probability, while an instrument also fixes the
post-measurement state. A first instrument uses
$K_0=|0\rangle\langle0|$ and $K_1=|1\rangle\langle1|$. Its effects are
$K_j^\dagger K_j=|j\rangle\langle j|$ and its nonzero conditional outputs
are $|j\rangle\langle j|$.

A second instrument uses $L_0=|+\rangle\langle0|$ and
$L_1=|+\rangle\langle1|$. Again
$L_j^\dagger L_j=|j\rangle\langle j|$, so both instruments return outcome
$j$ with probability $\rho_{jj}$. But now
$L_j\rho L_j^\dagger=\rho_{jj}|+\rangle\langle+|$; every allowed outcome
prepares $|+\rangle$. Each set obeys completeness because its effects sum
to $I$. The unconditional first instrument dephases, whereas the second
replaces every unit-trace input by $|+\rangle\langle+|$. An outcome of
zero probability has no normalized conditional state and requires no
separate prescription.

## Chapter 3: thermalization

The relevant distinction between dephasing and equilibrium is developed in
@sec-thermalization.

### Exercise 1: Degenerate spectrum

For $H=\operatorname{diag}(0,0,1)$ and $\hbar=1$,
$|\psi(t)\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle+e^{-it}|2\rangle)/\sqrt3$.
Every density-matrix entry evolves as
$\rho_{ab}(t)=e^{-it(E_a-E_b)}/3$. The infinite-time average of a
nonzero-frequency exponential is zero, while a zero-frequency entry
remains unchanged. Thus

$$
\overline\rho=\frac13
\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}
=\frac23|+_{01}\rangle\langle+_{01}|+\frac13|2\rangle\langle2|,
\quad |+_{01}\rangle=\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
$$ {#eq-sol-degenerate-average}

The coherence between $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$ survives because their
energies coincide. The basis-independent statement is
$\overline\rho=\sum_E P_E\rho(0)P_E$, with $P_E$ the full projector onto an
energy eigenspace. Deleting all off-diagonal entries in an arbitrarily
chosen degenerate eigenbasis would incorrectly delete a stationary
coherence. The surviving weights $2/3,1/3,0$ also show why the time average
need not be a Gibbs state.

### Exercise 3: Finite-bath correction

The probability for a system level of energy $E_a$ is proportional to the
bath density of states at $E_{\mathrm{tot}}-E_a$. Expand its entropy around
$E_{\mathrm{tot}}$:

$$
S_B(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-E_a)=S_B(E_{\mathrm{tot}})-\beta E_a
+\frac12 S_B''(E_{\mathrm{tot}})E_a^2+\cdots.
$$

With $k_B=1$, $\beta=1/T$ and $C_B=dE_B/dT$, the chain rule gives
$S_B''=d\beta/dE_B=-1/(T^2C_B)$. For a stable bath of positive heat
capacity,

$$
p_a\ \propto\ \exp\!\left[-\beta E_a-
\frac{E_a^2}{2T^2C_B}+\cdots\right].
$$ {#eq-sol-finite-bath}

The quadratic term suppresses large exchanges more strongly than an
infinite bath does. The local approximation should be centered on the
relevant exchange range: a shift of energy origin changes the expansion
point and the corresponding $\beta$ together. A sufficient condition is
$|\Delta E_a|^2/(T^2C_B)\ll1$ throughout the appreciably populated system
levels, together with small higher derivatives over that range. Merely
saying that the bath has many sites is insufficient near a singular
thermodynamic regime or when the system exchanges an extensive energy.

## Chapter 4: quantum designs

Use the Haar moment and frame-potential definitions in @sec-randomness-designs.

### Exercise 3: Tetrahedron

Choose the four unit vectors listed in the exercise, each divided by
$\sqrt3$ and sampled with probability $1/4$. Each Cartesian component has
two plus and two minus signs, so $\mathbb E r_i=0$. Each square is $1/3$,
while opposite signs cancel in every off-diagonal product. Therefore
$\mathbb E r_ir_j=\delta_{ij}/3$.

Expanding $P_{\boldsymbol r}=(I+\boldsymbol r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)/2$
shows that $\mathbb E P_{\boldsymbol r}^{\otimes2}$ depends only on these
first and second Bloch moments. They equal those of the sphere, proving
the 2-design property without assuming that four points are continuously
uniform. At third order, however, every listed vertex satisfies
$r_xr_yr_z=1/(3\sqrt3)$. The spherical average of this odd monomial is
zero, since inversion changes its sign and preserves the measure. Hence

$$
\operatorname{Tr}[(X\otimes Y\otimes Z)M^{(3)}_{\mathrm{tet}}]
=\frac1{3\sqrt3}\neq0
=\operatorname{Tr}[(X\otimes Y\otimes Z)M^{(3)}_{\mathrm H}].
$$ {#eq-sol-tetrahedron-witness}

This explicit three-copy witness proves failure at order three. Agreement
of the polarization covariance is a complete order-two test for qubits,
but says nothing about the cubic correlation just exposed.

### Exercise 4: Estimator bias

For $N$ independent samples from an ensemble $\mathcal E$, let
$\widehat F_k=N^{-2}\sum_{i,j}|\langle\psi_i|\psi_j\rangle|^{2k}$.
There are $N$ diagonal terms, each exactly one, and $N(N-1)$ off-diagonal
terms, each with expectation $F_k(\mathcal E)$. Therefore

$$
\mathbb E\widehat F_k=\frac1N+\left(1-\frac1N\right)F_k(\mathcal E),
\qquad
\widetilde F_k=\frac1{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\ne j}
|\langle\psi_i|\psi_j\rangle|^{2k}.
$$ {#eq-sol-unbiased-frame-estimator}

The second expression is unbiased for $N\geq2$. Excluding diagonal pairs
does not make the remaining terms independent: pairs sharing one sample
are correlated, so error bars must account for that dependence. Moreover,
the proof uses independently drawn labels. Sampling consecutive states
of a slowly mixing temporal trajectory can bias the off-diagonal average
as an estimator for an intended stationary ensemble. Removing self-pairs
corrects the algebraic sampling floor, rather than all finite-time or
correlation effects.

## Chapter 5: projected ensembles

The Born probabilities in @sec-projected-ensembles must be retained in
every average.

### Exercise 1: Unequal Schmidt weights

Let $0\leq\lambda\leq1$. Measuring $B$ in $Z$ gives $|0\rangle$ with
probability $\lambda$ and $|1\rangle$ with probability $1-\lambda$.
Measuring in $X$ instead gives the unnormalized vectors
$(\sqrt\lambda|0\rangle\pm\sqrt{1-\lambda}|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
Their squared norms are $1/2$, so the normalized states are
$|\phi_\pm\rangle=\sqrt\lambda|0\rangle\pm\sqrt{1-\lambda}|1\rangle$,
with equal probabilities. Both ensembles average to
$\rho_A=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,1-\lambda)$.

For the $Z$ ensemble, the random conditional expectation
$z_\psi=\langle Z\rangle_\psi$ takes values $\pm1$. Thus
$\mathbb E z_\psi=2\lambda-1$ and
$\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal E_Z}(z_\psi)=1-(2\lambda-1)^2=4\lambda(1-\lambda)$.
For the $X$ ensemble both states have $z_\psi=2\lambda-1$, so the ensemble
variance is zero. Their second raw moments are respectively $1$ and
$(2\lambda-1)^2$.

There is also a different variance: measuring $Z$ *within* an individual
conditional state. This quantum measurement variance is zero for each
$Z$-prepared state and $4\lambda(1-\lambda)$ for each $X$-prepared state.
Their roles exchange so that the total unconditioned measurement variance
is unchanged. Finally,
$\langle\phi_+|\phi_-\rangle=2\lambda-1$, which vanishes only for equal
Schmidt weights. Orthogonal bath outcomes do not require orthogonal
conditional states on the retained subsystem.

### Exercise 4: Finite-bath obstruction

Here $d_A=4$ and at most $d_B=8$ pure conditional states have nonzero
weight. A sum of eight rank-one replicated projectors has rank at most
eight. But the Haar $k$th moment is maximally mixed on a symmetric
subspace of dimension $D_k=\binom{k+3}{k}$. The first values are
$D_1=4$, $D_2=10$, and $D_3=20$. Consequently all exact design orders
$k\geq2$ are excluded; order one is allowed by rank, without being
guaranteed dynamically.

Let $P$ project onto the support of the actual third moment and let its
rank be $r\leq8$. A two-outcome measurement with effect $I-P$ returns zero
for that moment and $1-r/20$ for Haar. Since trace distance bounds every
effect's probability difference,

$$
\Delta_3\geq1-\frac r{20}\geq\frac35.
$$ {#eq-sol-small-bath-bound}

This bound is independent of scrambling quality. More evolution can
change the eight states, but cannot increase the number of possible
outcomes in this fixed rank-one measurement protocol.

## Chapter 6: constraints and symmetry

The thermodynamic assumptions behind constrained targets are discussed in
@sec-scrooge-symmetry.

### Exercise 5: Macroscopic input fluctuations

In a uniformly mixed fixed-charge sector with $Q=nN$, one site is occupied
with probability $n$. For two distinct sites,
$\langle n_1n_2\rangle=Q(Q-1)/[N(N-1)]\to n^2$. Thus any fixed pair tends
to the product Bernoulli state with probabilities
$((1-n)^2,n(1-n),n(1-n),n^2)$ in the basis $00,01,10,11$. The finite-size
negative covariance vanishes as $1/N$ when the filling is fixed.

At $n=1/2$, the one-site state is $I/2$ and the pair is $I/4$ in the
thermodynamic limit. For an equal incoherent average of sectors near
$n=1/4$ and $n=3/4$, the one-site state is again $I/2$. The pair instead is

$$
\rho_{12}\longrightarrow
\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac5{16},\frac3{16},\frac3{16},\frac5{16}\right),
\qquad
\langle n_1n_2\rangle-\langle n_1\rangle\langle n_2\rangle=\frac1{16}.
$$ {#eq-sol-macroscopic-charge-mixture}

The surviving covariance is the classical variance of the random filling,
$\mathbb E n^2-(\mathbb E n)^2$, rather than a failure to scramble inside
either sector. Replacing a broad charge distribution by its mean therefore
loses local two-site information even at infinite system size. An
assumption that charge fluctuations are subextensive rules out this
particular counterexample and must be stated before using one effective
filling for every finite subsystem.

### Exercise 6: Failure of a naive theorem composition

Choose $0<\epsilon<1/2$ and
$T=\operatorname{diag}(1-\epsilon^2,\epsilon^2)$,
$M=\operatorname{diag}(1-\epsilon^2-\epsilon,\epsilon^2+\epsilon)$.
Both are density matrices. Their difference is
$\operatorname{diag}(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$, so $D(M,T)=\epsilon\to0$.
Nevertheless the second basis vector sees relative error
$|M_{22}-T_{22}|/T_{22}=1/\epsilon$, which diverges.

Equivalently, the second eigenvalue of
$T^{-1/2}MT^{-1/2}-I$ is $1/\epsilon$. The first is
$-\epsilon/(1-\epsilon^2)$, so the operator norm of this relative error is
$1/\epsilon$. An additive trace-distance guarantee therefore cannot be
inserted without modification into a theorem requiring a small relative
operator error. A lower bound on $\lambda_{\min}(T)$, or a restriction to
its well-populated support, is additional information. The example is
especially relevant to low-temperature targets, where small eigenvalues
are physically natural.

## Chapter 7: Gaussian conditioning

Here vacuum quadrature covariance is $I/2$, as in @sec-gaussian-nonlocal.

### Exercise 2: Schur complement and purity

For the two-mode squeezed state, set $c=\cosh2r$, $s=\sinh2r$ and
$C=sZ/2$. A diagonal pure measurement seed has
$V_M=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})/2$ with $t=e^{2u}>0$.
The Schur complement gives diagonal conditional variances

$$
v_q=\frac12\left(c-\frac{s^2}{c+t}\right)
=\frac{1+ct}{2(c+t)},\qquad
v_p=\frac{1+c/t}{2(c+1/t)}.
$$ {#eq-sol-gaussian-seed-variances}

The simplification uses $s^2=c^2-1$. Multiplying the two expressions,
the numerator is
$(1+ct)(1+c/t)=1+c(t+t^{-1})+c^2$, which equals
$(c+t)(c+t^{-1})$. Therefore $v_qv_p=1/4$, the one-mode pure-state
condition in this convention. The outcome changes the conditional mean,
not these variances.

At $u=0$, $t=1$ and $v_q=v_p=1/2$, so the state is coherent and
$d_{A|y}=sZy/(c+1)$. At large $|u|$ the state can be squeezed while
remaining pure. The check separates purity from coherent-state form:
rank-one Gaussian measurements preserve conditional purity of a globally
pure pair, but do not all prepare the same covariance.

### Exercise 3: Homodyne information

In the coherent cloud the unknown displacement $d_q$ is a centered
Gaussian of variance $\overline n$. A homodyne reading is
$Q=d_q+\xi$ with independent vacuum noise
$\operatorname{Var}\xi=1/2$. A real Gaussian of variance $v$ has
differential entropy $h=\frac12\log(2\pi ev)$, so

$$
I(d_q;Q)=h(Q)-h(Q|d_q)=\frac12\log(1+2\overline n).
$$ {#eq-sol-homodyne-information}

The unobserved $d_p$ is independent and supplies no additional information
to this reading. Heterodyne measures both quadratures with noise variance
one in each and obtains $I_{\mathrm{het}}=\log(1+\overline n)$. At small
$\overline n$, the homodyne and heterodyne values are respectively
$\overline n-\overline n^2+\cdots$ and
$\overline n-\overline n^2/2+\cdots$. At large occupation they grow as
$\frac12\log(2\overline n)$ and $\log\overline n$. Heterodyne wins here
because the encoded signal occupies both independent quadratures;
homodyne's lower noise in one quadrature does not compensate for missing
the other. Indeed $(1+\overline n)^2\geq1+2\overline n$ establishes this
ordering for every $\overline n\geq0$.

## Chapter 8: Hilbert-space ergodicity

The temporal ensemble and its clock are specified in @sec-temporal-ergodicity.

### Exercise 2: Cross-observable covariances

Write $o=\langle\psi|O|\psi\rangle$ and
$q=\langle\psi|Q|\psi\rangle$. Their product is
$\operatorname{Tr}[(O\otimes Q)P_\psi^{\otimes2}]$. Inserting
$M_{\mathrm H}^{(2)}=(I+S)/[d(d+1)]$ gives
$\mathbb E_{\mathrm H}(oq)=[\operatorname{Tr}O\operatorname{Tr}Q+
\operatorname{Tr}(OQ)]/[d(d+1)]$. Since the first means are
$\operatorname{Tr}O/d$ and $\operatorname{Tr}Q/d$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathrm H}(o,q)=
\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(OQ)-\operatorname{Tr}O\operatorname{Tr}Q/d}
{d(d+1)}.
$$ {#eq-sol-haar-observable-covariance}

Subtracting the trace parts makes the numerator simply the
Hilbert–Schmidt inner product of the centered observables. For $Q=O$ it
is nonnegative, as a variance requires. For traceless orthogonal Paulis
the covariance vanishes; for a qubit Pauli with itself it equals $1/3$.
This concerns fluctuations of conditional *expectations* over pure
states, rather than the operator covariance of two potentially
noncommuting measurements on one state.

### Exercise 4: Rank and sample complexity

An empirical moment is
$M_T^{(k)}=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T|\psi_t\rangle^{\otimes k}
\langle\psi_t|^{\otimes k}$. Its image lies in the span of $T$ vectors,
so its rank $r$ cannot exceed $T$. All those vectors also lie in the
symmetric subspace. Let $P$ be the support projector. Then
$\operatorname{Tr}(PM_T^{(k)})=1$ and
$\operatorname{Tr}(PM_{\mathrm H}^{(k)})=r/D_k$.

The operational characterization
$D(\rho,\sigma)=\max_{0\leq E\leq I}|\operatorname{Tr}E(\rho-\sigma)|$
applied to $E=P$ yields
$\Delta_T^{(k)}\geq1-r/D_k\geq1-T/D_k$ when $T<D_k$.
Independence of the sampled states is unnecessary for this deterministic
rank bound. Random sampling cannot evade it, and strong temporal
correlations can only lower the actual rank. Since $D_k$ grows as
$d^k/k!$ for fixed $k$ and large $d$, a small scalar diagnostic obtained
from very few times cannot by itself certify small full moment distance.

## Chapter 9: aperiodic drives

Operator ordering follows the word convention of @sec-aperiodic-drives.

### Exercise 2: Derive the channel recursion

Let $X,Y$ have lengths $L_X,L_Y$ and let $R$ be an arbitrary replicated
input operator. The first $L_X$ sampled prefixes of $XY$ are exactly the
prefixes of $X$. A prefix at offset $r$ into $Y$ has total gate
$V_Y(r)V_X$, with the later operation on the left. Its action on $R$ is
$\mathcal V_Y(r)\circ\mathcal V_X(R)$. Splitting the sum and dividing by
$L_X+L_Y$ gives the concatenation formula in the chapter.

For three blocks, put $L=L_X+L_Y+L_Z$. Repeating the same argument gives

$$
\mathcal N_{XYZ}^{(k)}=
\frac{L_X}{L}\mathcal N_X^{(k)}+
\frac{L_Y}{L}\mathcal N_Y^{(k)}\circ\mathcal V_X^{(k)}+
\frac{L_Z}{L}\mathcal N_Z^{(k)}\circ\mathcal V_Y^{(k)}
\circ\mathcal V_X^{(k)}.
$$ {#eq-sol-three-block-channel}

The last term includes both complete earlier blocks, in their actual
time order. Including a block's endpoint as well as the next block's
initial point would count their boundary twice; the convention
$0\leq t<L_W$ prevents this. The weights sum to one, so the recurrence
preserves a normalized average. Nothing in this derivation assumes
random gates, ergodicity, or existence of an infinite-time limit.

### Exercise 6: A heavy-tailed clock

Treat the large recursion level $n$ as continuous for its tail and write
$p_n(n)\sim Cn^{-3/2}$. With $\tau=2^n$,
$n=\log\tau/\log2$ and $dn/d\tau=1/(\tau\log2)$. Probability transforms
with the Jacobian, giving

$$
p_\tau(\tau)\sim
\frac{C\sqrt{\log2}}{\tau(\log\tau)^{3/2}},\qquad
\Pr(\tau>t)\sim\frac{2C\sqrt{\log2}}{\sqrt{\log t}}.
$$ {#eq-sol-heavy-clock}

The survival function follows by substituting $x=\log\tau$ into its
tail integral. A nonnegative random variable has mean
$\int_0^\infty\Pr(\tau>t)\,dt$, which diverges for this survival law.
Equivalently, the discrete sum $\sum_n2^np_n(n)$ diverges. Thus a tail
that looks like an ordinary power law in recursion depth becomes
exceptionally broad in gate count. The calculation derives a consequence
of the assumed level distribution; it does not establish that every
aperiodic drive has this distribution or that different plateaus are
independent renewal events.

## Chapter 10: coherence and magic

All resource entropies in this section are in bits, following
@sec-resource-transitions.

### Exercise 2: Two-copy discrimination

The symmetric space splits into $d$ diagonal vectors $|aa\rangle$ and
$d(d-1)/2$ off-diagonal symmetric vectors
$(|ab\rangle+|ba\rangle)/\sqrt2$, $a<b$. On the first subspace,
$M_{\mathrm{bit}}^{(2)}-M_{\mathrm H}^{(2)}$ has eigenvalue
$(d-1)/[d(d+1)]$; on the second it has eigenvalue
$-2/[d(d+1)]$. The antisymmetric space contributes zero. Adding the
positive eigenvalues, or half the sum of all absolute eigenvalues,
gives $\Delta_2=(d-1)/(d+1)$.

For one, two, and three retained qubits, $d=2,4,8$, so the distances are
$1/3,3/5,7/9$. The effect projecting onto
$\operatorname{span}\{|aa\rangle\}$ achieves the optimal probability
difference: the classical ensemble always lands there, whereas Haar does
so with probability $2/(d+1)$. On a single copy both hypotheses are
$I/d$, so every effect has identical expectation. Increasing experimental
precision cannot extract a distinction that the first moment erases;
the experiment must access shared-label multi-copy information.

### Exercise 5: Coherence without magic

For a pure qubit, computational coherence is the binary entropy of its
$Z$ probabilities. Thus $C_r(|0\rangle)=0$, while $|+\rangle$,
$|Y_+\rangle$, and $|T\rangle$ each have $C_r=1$. To compute the second
stabilizer Rényi entropy, include the identity Pauli explicitly:

$$
M_2=-\log_2\!\left[\frac{1+r_x^4+r_y^4+r_z^4}{2}\right].
$$ {#eq-sol-qubit-magic}

The respective Bloch vectors are $(0,0,1)$, $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$ and
$(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2,0)$. The first three give bracket one and $M_2=0$.
The last gives bracket $3/4$ and
$M_2=\log_2(4/3)$. The complex amplitude in $|Y_+\rangle$ therefore
does not imply magic: it is a Pauli eigenstate and hence stabilizer.
Coherence detects superposition relative to a chosen basis, whereas
magic detects departure from the entire stabilizer set. The two
diagnostics answer different operational questions even on one qubit.

## Chapter 11: channels and bath records

The dilation and Kraus conventions are those of @sec-channels-memory.

### Exercise 1: Dephasing from a controlled bath rotation

Since $e^{-i\theta X}|0\rangle=\cos\theta|0\rangle-i\sin\theta|1\rangle$,
projection onto bath outputs gives
$K_0=|0\rangle\langle0|+\cos\theta|1\rangle\langle1|$ and
$K_1=-i\sin\theta|1\rangle\langle1|$. The effects sum to $I$. Direct
multiplication shows that populations are unchanged, while
$\rho_{01}\mapsto\cos\theta\,\rho_{01}$. This is exactly the overlap of
the two possible bath states, so lost coherence records the bath's
ability to distinguish the system basis states.

The channel is unitary precisely when $|\cos\theta|=1$, namely
$\theta\in\pi\mathbb Z$. For even multiples it is the identity; for odd
multiples it is conjugation by $Z$. If $|\cos\theta|<1$, an input
$|+\rangle$ has output Bloch length $|\cos\theta|<1$ and becomes mixed,
which rules out a unitary channel. At $\cos\theta=0$ the two bath states
are orthogonal and the channel completely dephases.

### Exercise 6: Radial diagnostics

Set $d=d_S$, $R=\|G\|_F^2$, and
$W=\|K\|_F^2=Y^2R/(dd_B)$. Each of the $d^2$ squared complex-Gaussian
entries has mean and variance one, so
$\mathbb ER=d^2$ and $\mathbb ER^2=d^2(d^2+1)$. Independence and
$\mathbb EY^2=1$, $\mathbb EY^4=e^{4\sigma^2}$ imply

$$
\mathbb EW=\frac d{d_B},\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{Var}W}{(\mathbb EW)^2}
=e^{4\sigma^2}\left(1+\frac1{d^2}\right)-1.
$$ {#eq-sol-kraus-radial-variation}

The coefficient of variation is the square root of the last expression.
It approaches $\sqrt{e^{4\sigma^2}-1}$ at fixed nonzero $\sigma$ as
$d\to\infty$. At $\sigma=0$ it is $1/d$, the ordinary Gaussian norm
concentration. Thus a fluctuating scalar can retain broad outcome norms
even when the many entries make the Gaussian radial factor sharply
concentrated. These are ensemble moments of the stated scaling model;
they do not assert that independent finite draws of $K$ satisfy exact
Kraus completeness for one physical instrument.

## Chapter 12: temporal memory

See @sec-temporal-entanglement for the difference between a normalized
history vector and a process Choi operator.

### Exercise 2: A memory bit

Prepare $|+\rangle$, let the bath apply $Z^b$, and measure $X$. The
recorded sign is deterministically $x_1=(-1)^b$. Now prepare a fresh
$|+\rangle$ regardless of that sign, repeat the interaction, and record
$x_2$. With a reused bath bit,
$p(x_1,x_2)=\frac12\delta_{x_1,x_2}$, so
$\mathbb E(x_1x_2)=1$. With independent unbiased bits at the two steps,
all four sign pairs have probability $1/4$ and
$\mathbb E(x_1x_2)=0$.

Each individual step has the same averaged complete-dephasing channel.
The difference appears only in a multi-time experiment that retains the
record and makes a causal break. After repreparation the system input is
identical in every run, yet the future is correlated with the earlier
record through the bath. This disproves memorylessness on the accessible
probe. It witnesses classical memory; no entanglement or quantum storage
is required for this particular violation.

### Exercise 4: MPS rank and approximation

The normalized Schmidt probabilities are $p_0=1/2$ and
$p_1=\cdots=p_D=1/(2D)$. For rank $r\geq1$, the optimal approximation
keeps the largest weight and $r-1$ of the equal smaller weights. Its
discarded weight is
$w_{\mathrm{disc}}=(D-r+1)/(2D)$. Requiring this to be at most $0.01$ gives

$$
r_{\min}=1+\lceil0.98D\rceil.
$$ {#eq-sol-schmidt-rank-required}

The formula includes the rounding needed when $D$ is small. Although
$S_2=-\log[(1+1/D)/4]\to\log4$, almost all of the $D$ small Schmidt
weights must be retained at this accuracy. If $D=e^{cT}$, the required
bond rank grows exponentially in time. “Discarded weight” here means the
squared norm lost by the unnormalized Schmidt truncation. Renormalizing
the truncated vector gives fidelity $1-w_{\mathrm{disc}}$ with the original
and pure-state trace distance $\sqrt{w_{\mathrm{disc}}}$; these different
error conventions should not be conflated. A bounded second Rényi
entropy alone does not control a prescribed approximation error.

## Chapter 13: constraints, scars, and fragments

The graph components and infinite-temperature inner product are defined
in @sec-scars-fragmentation.

### Exercise 1: Counting allowed states

Let $G(x)=\sum_{L\geq0}D_Lx^L$. Summing
$D_L=D_{L-1}+D_{L-2}$ for $L\geq2$ yields
$G-1-2x=x(G-1)+x^2G$. Keeping the initial conditions separately is what
fixes the numerator. Solving gives

$$
G(x)=\frac{1+x}{1-x-x^2}.
$$ {#eq-sol-blockade-generating-function}

The denominator roots are $x_+=(\sqrt5-1)/2=1/\varphi$ and
$x_-=-(1+\sqrt5)/2=-\varphi$. The positive root is closer to the origin,
and the numerator does not cancel it, so it determines the radius of
convergence and exponential growth $D_L\propto\varphi^L$. More precisely,
$D_L=F_{L+2}=[\varphi^{L+2}-(-1/\varphi)^{L+2}]/\sqrt5$. The constraint
reduces the entropy density from $\log2$ to $\log\varphi$ but still leaves
an exponentially large space. This counting fact does not decide whether
the Hamiltonian thermalizes inside that space.

### Exercise 5: A local memory bound

The $Q=2,P=7$ sector has three equally weighted basis states. Only the
frozen state $100001$ has $n_1=1$, hence
$\langle n_1\rangle=1/3$ and
$O=n_1-1/3=\operatorname{diag}(2/3,-1/3,-1/3)$. Its fragment averages are
$O_f=2/3$ and $O_a=-1/3$, with weights $w_f=1/3$, $w_a=2/3$. The bound is

$$
\overline C\geq\frac13\left(\frac23\right)^2+
\frac23\left(-\frac13\right)^2=\frac29.
$$ {#eq-sol-fragment-memory}

In fact $O$ is constant on each entire connected block, so it commutes
with the Hamiltonian restricted to this sector. Therefore
$C(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(O^2)/3=2/9$ for every time: the bound is
saturated. No dephasing calculation is needed. A generic local observable
need not be block-constant, and its conserved projection could be much
smaller. The example demonstrates explicitly how a local operator can
retain memory of an additional fragment label even after the two
specified global charges have been fixed.

## Chapter 14: driven phases

The small expansion parameter is local frequency times period, as
explained in @sec-driven-phases.

### Exercise 1: Sign of the engineered term

Put $U=e^{-iTH_B/2}e^{-iTH_A/2}$, with $A$ applied first. Direct
multiplication gives
$U=I-iT(H_A+H_B)/2-T^2(H_A^2+H_B^2)/8-T^2H_BH_A/4+O(T^3)$.
Now write $H_F=H_0+TH_1+O(T^2)$, where $H_0=(H_A+H_B)/2$. Expanding
$e^{-iTH_F}$ produces the quadratic term
$-iT^2H_1-T^2(H_A^2+H_AH_B+H_BH_A+H_B^2)/8$.
Matching coefficients cancels the two square terms and leaves
$-iH_1=-[H_B,H_A]/8$. Therefore

$$
H_F=\frac{H_A+H_B}{2}-\frac{iT}{8}[H_B,H_A]+O(T^2).
$$ {#eq-sol-drive-commutator}

Reversing the segments interchanges $A,B$ and flips the commutator sign.
Because $[H_B,H_A]^\dagger=-[H_B,H_A]$, multiplication by $-i$ makes the
correction Hermitian. This is a useful check on both its sign and its
physical admissibility. The omitted terms in $H_F$ are of order $T^2$,
although the gate comparison was made through order $T^2$ with a
remainder of order $T^3$.

### Exercise 6: Domain walls in one dimension

For $D=-J\sum_iZ_iZ_{i+1}$, a satisfied bond has energy $-J$ and a domain
wall has energy $+J$. In an open chain at zero field, the bond variables
are independent after choosing one boundary spin. A wall therefore has
probability
$p_{\mathrm{dw}}=e^{-\beta J}/(e^{\beta J}+e^{-\beta J})
=1/(1+e^{2\beta J})\sim e^{-2\beta J}$.

Across $r$ bonds, each wall reverses the spin sign. Independence gives
$\langle Z_iZ_{i+r}\rangle=(1-2p_{\mathrm{dw}})^r=(\tanh\beta J)^r$, so

$$
\xi^{-1}=-\log\tanh(\beta J),\qquad
\xi\sim\frac12e^{2\beta J}\quad(\beta J\gg1).
$$ {#eq-sol-ising-correlation-length}

A finite chain with $Lp_{\mathrm{dw}}\ll1$ is usually almost uniformly
magnetized in a snapshot and can display a convincing finite-size ordered
regime. Yet $\xi$ is finite for every nonzero temperature, so there is no
thermodynamic long-range Ising order in this nearest-neighbor model.
Periodic boundaries require an even total number of walls; that changes
finite-size statistics but not the infinite-chain correlation length.
For prethermal time-crystal claims, a long lifetime of an effective
Hamiltonian and the existence of its ordered phase are separate
requirements. A low wall density establishes a useful finite-size scale,
not an infinite-volume ordered phase by itself.
